questions.prompt: Which subatomic particle has a positive charge in an atom?
questions.correctAnswer: Proton
questions.explanation: Protons are positively charged particles found in the nucleus of an atom.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the structure of the atom using protons, neutrons and electrons.

questions.prompt: Which particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.correctAnswer: Protons and neutrons
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, while electrons occupy energy levels around the nucleus.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the structure of the atom using protons, neutrons and electrons.

questions.prompt: An atom has 11 protons. What is its atomic number?
questions.explanation: Atomic number is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus.
questions.learningOutcome: Determine atomic number from the number of protons in an atom.

questions.prompt: An atom has 8 protons and 8 neutrons. What is its mass number?
questions.explanation: Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons, so 8 + 8 = 16.
questions.learningOutcome: Determine the mass number of elements from protons and neutrons.

questions.prompt: A neutral atom has 13 protons. How many electrons does it have?
questions.correctAnswer: 13 electrons
questions.explanation: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate the number of protons and electrons in a neutral atom.

questions.prompt: Which electron arrangement is correct for magnesium with atomic number 12?
questions.explanation: Magnesium has 12 electrons arranged as 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second and 2 in the third.
questions.learningOutcome: Write electron arrangements for elements using the first 20 elements.

questions.prompt: Which element is a non-metal among the first 20 elements?
questions.correctAnswer: Oxygen
questions.explanation: Oxygen is a non-metal, while sodium, magnesium and calcium are metals.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify elements into metals and non-metals using selected examples.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why chlorine is classified as a non-metal?
options: It has non-metal properties and is not a good conductor
It is shiny and easily hammered into sheets
It is used to make steel bridges
questions.correctAnswer: It has non-metal properties and is not a good conductor
questions.explanation: Non-metals usually have poor electrical conductivity and do not show typical metallic properties such as malleability.
questions.learningOutcome: Use properties to classify elements into metals and non-metals.

questions.prompt: An atom has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.correctAnswer: 18 neutrons
questions.explanation: Number of neutrons is mass number minus atomic number, so 35 - 17 = 18.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate the number of neutrons from mass number and atomic number.

questions.prompt: Which model would best represent the electron arrangement of carbon, atomic number 6?
options: Two electrons in the first shell and four in the second
Six electrons all in the first shell
Four electrons in the first shell and two in the second
Two protons outside the nucleus and four inside
questions.correctAnswer: Two electrons in the first shell and four in the second
questions.explanation: Carbon has six electrons, arranged as 2,4 in the first two energy levels.
questions.learningOutcome: Draw or interpret electron arrangement diagrams for selected atoms.

questions.prompt: Which plan would help a group make a simple atom model from locally available materials?
options: Use labelled beads for protons, neutrons and electrons, then place electrons on shells
Mix all beads in a tin without labels
Use only one bead to represent every particle in every atom
Draw a plant leaf and call it an atom
questions.correctAnswer: Use labelled beads for protons, neutrons and electrons, then place electrons on shells
questions.explanation: A useful model should show the nucleus particles clearly and place electrons on energy levels around the nucleus.
questions.learningOutcome: Create a model showing the atomic structure of selected elements.

questions.prompt: Which property describes most metals?
options: They conduct heat and electricity well
They are always gases at room temperature
They dissolve in water to form sugar
They cannot be shaped into wires
questions.correctAnswer: They conduct heat and electricity well
questions.explanation: Most metals are good conductors of heat and electricity and can often be shaped into useful forms.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe common physical properties of metals.

questions.prompt: What does malleability mean when describing a metal?
options: The ability to be hammered into sheets
The ability to kill germs in water
questions.correctAnswer: The ability to be hammered into sheets
questions.explanation: A malleable material can be beaten or pressed into thin sheets without breaking easily.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe common physical properties of metals.

questions.prompt: Which alloy is mainly made from copper and zinc?
questions.correctAnswer: Brass
questions.explanation: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, commonly used for fittings and decorative items.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the composition of common alloys.

questions.prompt: Which alloy is mainly made from iron and carbon?
questions.correctAnswer: Steel
questions.explanation: Steel is an alloy made mainly from iron with carbon added to improve useful properties.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the composition of common alloys.

questions.prompt: Why is copper commonly used in electrical wiring?
options: It is a good electrical conductor and can be drawn into wires
It is a poor conductor and breaks easily
It is a gas that fills the wire
It stops all electric current from flowing
questions.correctAnswer: It is a good electrical conductor and can be drawn into wires
questions.explanation: Copper conducts electricity well and is ductile, so it can be drawn into wires.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify uses of metals and alloys in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: Which conditions encourage rusting of iron?
options: Placing iron in dry nitrogen only
questions.correctAnswer: Presence of water and oxygen
questions.explanation: Iron rusts when it reacts with oxygen in the presence of water or moisture.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the causes of rusting in metals.

questions.prompt: Which method helps prevent rusting of a steel gate?
options: Pouring salty water on it daily
questions.correctAnswer: Painting the surface
questions.explanation: Paint forms a barrier that reduces contact between the iron in steel, oxygen and moisture.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain methods of preventing rusting of metals.

questions.prompt: A cooking utensil must resist rusting and be easy to clean. Which material is most suitable?
questions.correctAnswer: Stainless steel
questions.explanation: Stainless steel resists corrosion better than untreated iron and is suitable for many kitchen utensils.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify uses of metals and alloys in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: Why are alloys often preferred to pure metals for some uses?
options: They can have improved strength, hardness or resistance to corrosion
They are always lighter than air
They are never made from metals
They cannot be shaped into useful objects
questions.correctAnswer: They can have improved strength, hardness or resistance to corrosion
questions.explanation: Alloying can improve properties such as strength, hardness and resistance to corrosion.
questions.learningOutcome: Appreciate the importance of common alloys in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: A bicycle chain has turned reddish-brown after being left in the rain. What has most likely happened?
options: Iron in the chain has rusted
The chain has changed into plastic
The chain has become a non-metal
questions.correctAnswer: Iron in the chain has rusted
questions.explanation: The reddish-brown substance is rust, which forms when iron reacts with oxygen and moisture.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the effects of rusting of metals.

questions.prompt: Which investigation would best compare electrical conductivity of metals and non-metals safely?
options: Use a low-voltage cell, bulb and switch to test small samples in a simple circuit
Connect unknown samples directly to mains electricity
Heat all samples in a closed plastic bottle
Taste each sample to identify it
questions.correctAnswer: Use a low-voltage cell, bulb and switch to test small samples in a simple circuit
questions.explanation: A low-voltage circuit can show whether a material conducts electricity while reducing safety risk.
questions.learningOutcome: Investigate physical properties of metals using safe scientific procedures.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes pure water under normal classroom conditions?
options: It is colourless, odourless and tasteless
It is always blue and salty
It has a strong smell of metal
questions.correctAnswer: It is colourless, odourless and tasteless
questions.explanation: Pure water is commonly described as colourless, odourless and tasteless.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the physical properties of water.

questions.prompt: Which observation suggests that a water sample is hard water?
options: It forms scum and lathers poorly with soap
It instantly turns into ice at room temperature
It has no dissolved substances at all
questions.correctAnswer: It forms scum and lathers poorly with soap
questions.explanation: Hard water reacts with soap to form scum and produces little lather.
questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish between hard and soft water using lathering ability.

questions.prompt: Which method can soften temporary hard water?
questions.correctAnswer: Boiling
questions.explanation: Boiling can remove temporary hardness by changing dissolved hydrogen carbonates into insoluble carbonates.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply methods of softening temporary hard water in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: Why does soft water save soap during washing?
options: It lathers easily and does not form much scum with soap
It always contains large pieces of soil
It prevents any water from touching clothes
questions.correctAnswer: It lathers easily and does not form much scum with soap
questions.explanation: Soft water forms lather readily, so less soap is wasted forming scum.
questions.learningOutcome: Outline advantages of soft water in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: Which disadvantage is associated with hard water in kettles and boilers?
options: It can form scale that reduces heating efficiency
It makes water burn without heat
questions.correctAnswer: It can form scale that reduces heating efficiency
questions.explanation: Hard water can deposit scale, which wastes heat and may damage heating equipment.
questions.learningOutcome: Outline disadvantages of hard water in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: A learner tests two water samples with the same amount of soap. Sample A lathers quickly, while Sample B forms scum. Which conclusion is best?
options: Sample A is softer than Sample B
Sample B is pure distilled water
Sample A has more hardness than Sample B
Both samples are identical in hardness
questions.correctAnswer: Sample A is softer than Sample B
questions.explanation: Water that lathers more easily with soap is softer than water that forms scum.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare hard and soft water using experimental observations.

questions.prompt: Which plan is safest when comparing the taste of water from different sources?
options: Taste only water confirmed safe for drinking and use other observations for unsafe sources
Taste every sample from drains, rivers and taps equally
Boil water in a plastic bag over a strong flame
Use taste as the only test for water quality
questions.correctAnswer: Taste only water confirmed safe for drinking and use other observations for unsafe sources
questions.explanation: Only safe drinking water should be tasted; unsafe samples can be observed without tasting.
questions.learningOutcome: Investigate physical properties of water while observing safety precautions.

questions.prompt: Which organelle in plant cells contains chlorophyll for photosynthesis?
questions.correctAnswer: Chloroplast
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate the structure of chloroplasts to their role in photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which raw materials are needed for photosynthesis?
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon (IV) oxide and water
questions.explanation: Plants use carbon (IV) oxide and water to make glucose during photosynthesis.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify the raw materials and products of photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which products are formed during photosynthesis?
questions.correctAnswer: Glucose and oxygen
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis produces glucose as food and releases oxygen as a by-product.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify the raw materials and products of photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Why are leaves broad and thin in many plants?
options: To provide a large surface area for absorbing light and gases
To make them sink faster in water
To store stones inside the plant
questions.correctAnswer: To provide a large surface area for absorbing light and gases
questions.explanation: Broad, thin leaves expose more surface area to light and allow gases to diffuse over short distances.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain adaptations of the leaf to photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of testing a leaf with iodine solution after removing its green colour?
questions.correctAnswer: To test for starch
questions.explanation: Iodine solution turns blue-black if starch is present in the leaf.
questions.learningOutcome: Carry out an experiment to test for the presence of starch in a leaf.

questions.prompt: A destarched plant is placed in bright light with one leaf partly covered by black paper. Which part should test positive for starch?
options: The uncovered part exposed to light
questions.correctAnswer: The uncovered part exposed to light
questions.explanation: The uncovered part receives light and can photosynthesise, producing starch.
questions.learningOutcome: Investigate conditions necessary for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Why is photosynthesis important in food production?
options: It makes food in green plants that other organisms can use
It turns all animals into plants
It removes every gas from air
It changes hard water into rust
questions.correctAnswer: It makes food in green plants that other organisms can use
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis produces plant food and supports feeding relationships in ecosystems and agriculture.
questions.learningOutcome: Discuss the importance of photosynthesis in nature.

questions.prompt: A variegated leaf has green and white parts. After exposure to light, where is starch most likely found?
options: Mainly in the green parts because they contain chlorophyll
Only in the white parts because they lack chlorophyll
Equally in the cut stalk only
Nowhere because leaves cannot make food
questions.correctAnswer: Mainly in the green parts because they contain chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Green parts contain chlorophyll, so they can absorb light for photosynthesis and make starch.
questions.learningOutcome: Investigate the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which plan would best test whether carbon (IV) oxide is necessary for photosynthesis?
options: Grow one destarched leaf in air with carbon (IV) oxide removed and another in normal air, then test both for starch
Put both leaves in the dark and test immediately
Paint both leaves green and compare their colour
Place one leaf in hard water and one in soft water only
questions.correctAnswer: Grow one destarched leaf in air with carbon (IV) oxide removed and another in normal air, then test both for starch
questions.explanation: A fair test changes carbon (IV) oxide availability while keeping other conditions similar, then compares starch formation.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a fair experiment on conditions necessary for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which mode of nutrition describes an animal feeding on ready-made food and digesting it internally?
questions.correctAnswer: Holozoic nutrition
questions.explanation: Holozoic nutrition involves taking in solid or liquid food, digesting it and absorbing nutrients.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe modes of nutrition in animals.

questions.prompt: Which teeth are mainly used for cutting and biting food?
questions.correctAnswer: Incisors
questions.explanation: Incisors have chisel-like edges suited for biting and cutting food.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify types of teeth and their functions.

questions.prompt: Which teeth are best adapted for grinding food?
questions.correctAnswer: Molars
questions.explanation: Molars have broad surfaces that crush and grind food during chewing.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify types of teeth and their functions.

questions.prompt: Which term describes animals with different types of teeth such as incisors, canines and molars?
questions.correctAnswer: Heterodont
questions.explanation: Heterodont dentition means having different types of teeth with different functions.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe dentition in animals using homodont and heterodont examples.

questions.prompt: What happens during ingestion in human digestion?
options: Food is taken into the mouth
questions.correctAnswer: Food is taken into the mouth
questions.explanation: Ingestion is the taking in of food through the mouth before digestion continues.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe stages in the process of digestion in human beings.

questions.prompt: Which stage of digestion involves soluble nutrients moving into the bloodstream?
questions.correctAnswer: Absorption
questions.explanation: Absorption is the movement of digested soluble nutrients from the small intestine into the blood.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe stages in the process of digestion in human beings.

questions.prompt: Why does a herbivore such as a cow need broad grinding teeth?
options: To grind plant material before swallowing
To reflect light into the eye
questions.correctAnswer: To grind plant material before swallowing
questions.explanation: Herbivores feed on plant material, so broad molars and premolars help crush and grind their food.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate dentition to feeding habits in animals.

questions.prompt: Which example shows a parasitic mode of nutrition?
options: A tick feeding on blood from a cow
A maize plant making food in sunlight
A lion chewing meat after hunting
questions.correctAnswer: A tick feeding on blood from a cow
questions.explanation: A parasite obtains food from a host and may harm the host in the process.
questions.learningOutcome: Differentiate modes of nutrition in animals and related organisms.

questions.prompt: A learner says absorption and assimilation mean the same thing. Which response best corrects this?
options: Absorption moves nutrients into blood, while assimilation uses nutrients in body cells
Absorption removes faeces, while assimilation means chewing
Both words mean oxygen leaving a leaf
Both words describe rusting of metals
questions.correctAnswer: Absorption moves nutrients into blood, while assimilation uses nutrients in body cells
questions.explanation: Absorption and assimilation are related but different stages in nutrition.
questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish between digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion.

questions.prompt: Which comparison correctly matches an animal with likely dentition?
options: Carnivore - sharp canines for tearing flesh
Herbivore - no grinding teeth for plants
Omnivore - only one type of tooth
Carnivore - flat molars only and no canines
questions.correctAnswer: Carnivore - sharp canines for tearing flesh
questions.explanation: Carnivores usually have strong canines that help grip and tear flesh.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze dentition in relation to feeding habits in animals.

questions.prompt: Which part of a flower produces pollen grains?
questions.correctAnswer: Anther
questions.explanation: The anther is part of the stamen and produces pollen grains.
questions.learningOutcome: Outline the functions of parts of a flower.

questions.prompt: Which part of a flower receives pollen during pollination?
questions.correctAnswer: Stigma
questions.explanation: The stigma is the receptive part of the carpel where pollen lands during pollination.
questions.learningOutcome: Outline the functions of parts of a flower.

questions.prompt: What is pollination in flowering plants?
options: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
Movement of food through the oesophagus
Softening of hard water by boiling
questions.correctAnswer: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
questions.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe pollination in plants.

questions.prompt: Which feature is common in insect-pollinated flowers?
options: Brightly coloured petals or scent to attract insects
Tiny dull petals with no nectar and exposed stamens only
questions.correctAnswer: Brightly coloured petals or scent to attract insects
questions.explanation: Insect-pollinated flowers often attract insects using colour, scent or nectar.
questions.learningOutcome: Outline adaptations of flowers to insect pollination.

questions.prompt: Which feature helps wind-pollinated flowers release and catch pollen?
questions.correctAnswer: Light pollen and feathery stigmas
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers often produce light pollen and have feathery stigmas to trap wind-borne pollen.
questions.learningOutcome: Outline adaptations of flowers to wind pollination.

questions.prompt: What happens during fertilisation in flowering plants?
options: A male gamete fuses with a female gamete in the ovule
A leaf tests positive for iodine
A seed is blown away by wind
Soap forms lather in soft water
questions.correctAnswer: A male gamete fuses with a female gamete in the ovule
questions.explanation: Fertilisation occurs when male and female gametes fuse, leading to seed formation.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain fertilisation in flowering plants.

questions.prompt: After fertilisation in a flowering plant, what does the ovule usually develop into?
questions.correctAnswer: Seed
questions.explanation: After fertilisation, the ovule develops into a seed while the ovary may develop into a fruit.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain seed and fruit formation in flowering plants.

questions.prompt: Which fruit is adapted for dispersal by animals because it is fleshy and edible?
questions.correctAnswer: Mango
questions.explanation: Fleshy fruits such as mango can be eaten by animals, helping seeds move away from the parent plant.
questions.learningOutcome: Categorise fruits and seeds based on their mode of dispersal.

questions.prompt: Which seed adaptation is most useful for wind dispersal?
options: Light weight with wing-like or hair-like structures
Heavy smooth stone with no air resistance
Bright petals attached to a tooth
A thick iron coat that rusts easily
questions.correctAnswer: Light weight with wing-like or hair-like structures
questions.explanation: Light seeds with wings or hairs can be carried away by moving air.
questions.learningOutcome: Categorise fruits and seeds based on their mode of dispersal.

questions.prompt: Which statement best compares self-pollination and cross-pollination?
options: Self-pollination uses pollen from the same plant, while cross-pollination uses pollen from another plant of the same species
Self-pollination happens only in animals, while cross-pollination happens only in metals
Self-pollination forms rust, while cross-pollination softens water
Both processes mean seed dispersal by wind
questions.correctAnswer: Self-pollination uses pollen from the same plant, while cross-pollination uses pollen from another plant of the same species
questions.explanation: The difference depends on whether pollen comes from the same plant or from a different plant of the same species.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe types of pollination in plants.

questions.prompt: How can careless use of agrochemicals reduce reproduction in flowering plants?
options: It can kill pollinating insects that transfer pollen
It makes all seeds germinate instantly
It prevents all plants from needing light
questions.correctAnswer: It can kill pollinating insects that transfer pollen
questions.explanation: Some agrochemicals can harm pollinators, reducing pollination and seed or fruit formation.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain factors that affect reproduction in flowering plants.

questions.prompt: Which activity would best show the importance of flowers in nature without damaging the environment?
options: Observe and record visiting pollinators on living flowers without uprooting the plants
Cut all flowers in a school garden to count them
Spray unknown chemicals on flowers before observing
Remove all insects from the area permanently
questions.correctAnswer: Observe and record visiting pollinators on living flowers without uprooting the plants
questions.explanation: Observation protects plants and pollinators while helping learners connect flowers with pollination and biodiversity.
questions.learningOutcome: Recognise the role of flowers in nature through responsible investigation.

questions.prompt: Which item is a biotic component of an environment?
questions.correctAnswer: Grass
questions.explanation: Biotic components are living things, and grass is a living plant.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain biotic and abiotic factors of the environment.

questions.prompt: Which item is an abiotic factor in an ecosystem?
questions.correctAnswer: Water
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are non-living environmental factors such as water, light, temperature and pH.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain biotic and abiotic factors of the environment.

questions.prompt: Which relationship describes a lion hunting a zebra for food?
questions.correctAnswer: Predation
questions.explanation: Predation is a feeding relationship where one organism hunts and eats another.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain biotic interrelationships in an ecosystem.

questions.prompt: Which relationship occurs when two organisms use the same limited resource such as food or space?
questions.correctAnswer: Competition
questions.explanation: Competition occurs when organisms need the same limited resource in an environment.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain biotic interrelationships in an ecosystem.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is a correct food chain?
questions.correctAnswer: Grass -> grasshopper -> lizard -> hawk
questions.explanation: Energy flows from a producer to herbivores and then to higher-level consumers.
questions.learningOutcome: Construct food chains in the environment.

questions.prompt: What is the role of decomposers in an ecosystem?
options: They break down dead matter and recycle nutrients
They make all food chains begin with carnivores
They stop plants from needing minerals
questions.correctAnswer: They break down dead matter and recycle nutrients
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down dead organisms and wastes, returning nutrients to the environment.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the role of decomposers in an ecosystem.

questions.prompt: Which human activity can directly destroy habitats?
options: Planting indigenous trees on bare land
Using manure to improve soil responsibly
questions.correctAnswer: Clearing forest without proper conservation
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled clearing removes shelter and food sources for many organisms.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe effects of human activities on the environment.

questions.prompt: A fish species survives only in a narrow range of water salinity. Which abiotic factor is limiting its distribution?
questions.correctAnswer: Salinity
questions.explanation: Salinity is a non-living chemical factor that can affect where aquatic organisms survive.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain how abiotic factors affect living organisms.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains energy flow in a food web?
options: Energy enters through producers and passes to consumers along feeding links
Energy starts with top carnivores and always increases down the food chain
Energy is made by decomposers only and never reaches plants
Energy flow is the same as rusting iron
questions.correctAnswer: Energy enters through producers and passes to consumers along feeding links
questions.explanation: Producers capture energy, usually from sunlight, and this energy moves through consumers in food chains and webs.
questions.learningOutcome: Construct and interpret food webs in the environment.

questions.prompt: In a garden food web, birds feed on caterpillars and caterpillars feed on cabbages. What may happen first if most birds disappear?
options: Caterpillar numbers may increase and damage more cabbages
Cabbages will immediately eat the caterpillars
Water hardness will increase in the leaves
questions.correctAnswer: Caterpillar numbers may increase and damage more cabbages
questions.explanation: Removing a predator can allow its prey to increase, which may affect the plants they feed on.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze interdependence between organisms in food webs.

questions.prompt: Which plan best reduces the negative effect of human activities on a school compound ecosystem?
options: Separate waste, compost biodegradable matter, plant suitable trees and avoid destroying habitats
Burn all waste near classrooms every day
Remove every insect and flowering plant
Pour used oil into the soil to kill weeds
questions.correctAnswer: Separate waste, compost biodegradable matter, plant suitable trees and avoid destroying habitats
questions.explanation: The plan conserves habitats, recycles nutrients and reduces pollution.
questions.learningOutcome: Create practical ways of conserving interdependence in the environment.

questions.prompt: Which mirror curves inward like the inside of a spoon?
questions.correctAnswer: Concave mirror
questions.explanation: A concave mirror has a reflecting surface that curves inward.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe types of curved mirrors.

questions.prompt: Which mirror curves outward like the back of a spoon?
questions.correctAnswer: Convex mirror
questions.explanation: A convex mirror has a reflecting surface that bulges outward.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe types of curved mirrors.

questions.prompt: Which mirror is commonly used in vehicles to give a wide field of view?
questions.correctAnswer: Convex mirror
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors form small upright images and allow drivers to see a wider area.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain uses of convex mirrors in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: Which mirror can be used in a solar cooker to concentrate sunlight at a point?
questions.correctAnswer: Concave mirror
questions.explanation: A concave mirror can converge parallel rays of sunlight toward a focus.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain uses of concave mirrors in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: What is the principal axis of a curved mirror?
options: The straight line passing through the pole and centre of curvature
The rough edge of the mirror frame
Any random line drawn on a table
questions.correctAnswer: The straight line passing through the pole and centre of curvature
questions.explanation: The principal axis is the reference line through the pole and centre of curvature of a curved mirror.
questions.learningOutcome: Use terms associated with curved mirrors correctly.

questions.prompt: Which image is usually formed by a convex mirror?
questions.correctAnswer: Upright, diminished and virtual
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors usually form upright, smaller and virtual images.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe characteristics of images formed by convex mirrors.

questions.prompt: A learner wants to see an enlarged upright image of the face while shaving. Which mirror is most suitable when the face is close to it?
questions.correctAnswer: Concave mirror
questions.explanation: A concave mirror can form an enlarged upright virtual image when the object is placed close to the mirror.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply image characteristics of concave mirrors to day-to-day uses.

questions.prompt: Why is a convex mirror useful at a blind corner in a school driveway?
options: It gives a wider view of approaching people or vehicles
It focuses all light into one hot point
It changes sound waves into water waves
questions.correctAnswer: It gives a wider view of approaching people or vehicles
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors increase the field of view, which improves safety at corners.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain applications of curved mirrors in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: Which drawing instruction is best when constructing a ray diagram for a curved mirror?
options: Use a ruler, mark the principal axis, pole and focus, then draw rays with arrow directions
Avoid showing where the object is placed
Use only coloured shading without lines
questions.correctAnswer: Use a ruler, mark the principal axis, pole and focus, then draw rays with arrow directions
questions.explanation: A clear ray diagram needs labelled reference points, straight rays and direction arrows.
questions.learningOutcome: Draw ray diagrams to locate images formed by curved mirrors.

questions.prompt: What is a wave in science?
options: A disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another
questions.correctAnswer: A disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another
questions.explanation: A wave carries energy through a medium or through space without transporting matter overall.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe the generation of waves in nature.

questions.prompt: Which example shows a transverse wave?
options: A wave on a rope moving up and down as the wave travels along
questions.correctAnswer: A wave on a rope moving up and down as the wave travels along
questions.explanation: In a transverse wave, particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of wave travel.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify waves as longitudinal and transverse.

questions.prompt: Which example shows a longitudinal wave?
options: Light wave in a vacuum only
questions.correctAnswer: Sound wave travelling through air
questions.explanation: Sound in air is longitudinal because air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify waves as longitudinal and transverse.

questions.prompt: What is wavelength?
options: Distance between two successive crests or two successive troughs
Number of protons in an atom
Amount of soap used in hard water
questions.correctAnswer: Distance between two successive crests or two successive troughs
questions.explanation: Wavelength is the distance between matching points on consecutive waves.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe basic characteristics of waves in nature.

questions.prompt: What does frequency of a wave measure?
options: Number of complete waves passing a point each second
Distance from a mirror to its pole
Number of petals on a flower
Amount of rust on a nail
questions.correctAnswer: Number of complete waves passing a point each second
questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point per second and is measured in hertz.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe basic characteristics of waves in nature.

questions.prompt: Which equation relates wave speed, wavelength and frequency?
options: Wave speed = atomic number + mass number
Wave speed = pollen divided by stigma
questions.correctAnswer: Wave speed = wavelength x frequency
questions.explanation: For waves, speed is calculated by multiplying wavelength by frequency.
questions.learningOutcome: Use the wave equation to relate speed, wavelength and frequency.

questions.prompt: A wave has wavelength 2 m and frequency 5 Hz. What is its speed?
questions.correctAnswer: 10 m/s
questions.explanation: Wave speed = wavelength x frequency, so 2 m x 5 Hz = 10 m/s.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate wave speed using wavelength and frequency.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour occurs when waves bounce off a barrier?
questions.correctAnswer: Reflection
questions.explanation: Reflection occurs when waves bounce back after meeting a surface or barrier.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe basic characteristics of waves in nature.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour describes waves bending as they pass from one medium to another?
questions.correctAnswer: Refraction
questions.explanation: Refraction is the bending of waves when their speed changes as they enter another medium.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe basic characteristics of waves in nature.

questions.prompt: What is remote sensing?
options: Collecting information about an object or area from a distance using waves
Touching every object directly before observing it
Making an alloy from copper and zinc
questions.correctAnswer: Collecting information about an object or area from a distance using waves
questions.explanation: Remote sensing uses waves, often electromagnetic waves, to gather information without direct contact.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe remote sensing in relation to waves.

questions.prompt: Which application uses waves in medical diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswer: Ultrasound imaging
questions.explanation: Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to form images inside the body.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe applications of waves in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: Which application uses electromagnetic waves for communication?
questions.correctAnswer: Radio transmission
questions.explanation: Radio transmission uses electromagnetic waves to carry signals over distances.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe applications of waves in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: A drone maps crop health by detecting reflected radiation from plants. Which science idea is being applied?
questions.correctAnswer: Remote sensing using waves
questions.explanation: The drone collects information from a distance by detecting waves reflected or emitted by crops.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze remote sensing in relation to waves and day-to-day applications.

questions.prompt: A microwave oven warms food. Which energy transfer idea is involved?
options: Microwaves transfer energy to water molecules in the food
Hard water changes to soft water without heating
Pollen moves from anther to stigma
questions.correctAnswer: Microwaves transfer energy to water molecules in the food
questions.explanation: Microwave ovens use electromagnetic waves that transfer energy to molecules in food, causing heating.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain applications of waves in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: Which comparison correctly distinguishes transverse and longitudinal waves?
options: Transverse vibrations are perpendicular to travel direction, while longitudinal vibrations are parallel
Transverse waves have no energy, while longitudinal waves are always metals
Transverse waves occur only in digestion, while longitudinal waves occur only in flowers
Both wave types require rusting to move
questions.correctAnswer: Transverse vibrations are perpendicular to travel direction, while longitudinal vibrations are parallel
questions.explanation: The classification depends on the direction of vibration compared with the direction of wave travel.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify waves as longitudinal and transverse.

questions.prompt: A learner makes waves in a rope and doubles the frequency while wavelength stays the same. What happens to wave speed?
questions.correctAnswer: It doubles
questions.explanation: Since speed = wavelength x frequency, doubling frequency while wavelength is constant doubles the speed.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze the relationship between wavelength, frequency and wave speed.

questions.prompt: Which classroom activity safely demonstrates a longitudinal wave?
options: Push and pull one end of a slinky spring to create compressions and rarefactions
Look directly at the sun with a mirror
Connect a speaker to mains electricity using bare wires
Boil water in a sealed glass bottle
questions.correctAnswer: Push and pull one end of a slinky spring to create compressions and rarefactions
questions.explanation: A slinky can safely show compressions and rarefactions moving along the same direction as the vibration.
questions.learningOutcome: Create safe activities to demonstrate generation and classification of waves.

questions.prompt: Which safety rule is important when learning about X-rays and other high-energy waves?
options: Use them only under trained supervision and avoid unnecessary exposure
Use X-rays for entertainment at home
Stand near X-ray machines without protection for a long time
Point high-energy waves at classmates to see what happens
questions.correctAnswer: Use them only under trained supervision and avoid unnecessary exposure
questions.explanation: High-energy waves such as X-rays can be harmful, so exposure must be controlled by trained personnel.
questions.learningOutcome: Appreciate safe applications of waves in day-to-day life.

questions.prompt: A weather satellite observes cloud patterns over Kenya from space. Which process explains how it gathers information?
options: Remote sensing by detecting waves from Earth
Direct tasting of clouds by the satellite
Boiling the atmosphere to make soft water
Using flower petals to catch pollen
questions.correctAnswer: Remote sensing by detecting waves from Earth
questions.explanation: Weather satellites collect wave signals from a distance to infer information about clouds and weather.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyze remote sensing applications in weather and environmental monitoring.

questions.prompt: A group must design a poster on useful waves in the community. Which set of examples is most accurate?
options: Radio for communication, ultrasound for medical imaging, and microwaves for cooking
Rusting for communication, pollen for X-rays, and molars for Wi-Fi
Hard water for television, starch for MRI scans, and brass for sound
Seed dispersal for radar, digestion for radio, and rust for ultrasound
questions.correctAnswer: Radio for communication, ultrasound for medical imaging, and microwaves for cooking
questions.explanation: Those examples correctly match wave applications with communication, medicine and cooking.
questions.learningOutcome: Create summaries of applications of waves in day-to-day life.
